one: A request can be answered from a cache at many layers: browser, service worker, CDN, reverse proxy, application memory, Redis, and the database's own buffer cache.
an: Keeping snacks in your pocket, your desk, the office kitchen and the supermarket. The closer the cache, the faster, and the harder to keep fresh.
how: From the user outward: browser HTTP cache (plus a service worker, if the app has one) → CDN edge → reverse proxy (nginx, Varnish) → app memory → shared cache like Redis → the database's own buffer cache.
Each layer has a different scope: the browser cache belongs to one user; the CDN, reverse proxy and Redis are shared by all users; app memory belongs to one server process.
Measure hit rate, the share of requests a layer answers itself. A cache with a 5% hit rate is mostly overhead and staleness risk.
why: The fastest request is one that never reaches your server. Senior engineers pick the right layer for each kind of data.
trade: "There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things." Every cache adds staleness and another place for bugs to hide.

myth.m: When something is slow, add a cache.
myth.r: First find why it is slow (missing index, N+1). Caching a bad query hides it until the cache misses, then everything falls over at once.

q.s: A user's private dashboard data should be cached. Which layer is wrong for it?
o: The browser (Cache-Control: private)
Redis keyed by user ID
A shared CDN cache keyed only by URL
App memory keyed by user ID
q.e: A shared cache keyed by URL alone can serve one user's private data to another.

more: Memoization inside a request (per-request caches, React cache())
Measuring hit ratio and the cost of a miss
lab: Take one slow endpoint and add caching at three layers in turn: HTTP Cache-Control, an in-memory LRU, and Redis. Measure latency and DB queries for each.
Write down, for each layer, what happens when the data changes and how long a user could see stale data.

plain:
A cache is a saved copy of a result, so you do not have to compute or fetch it again. Caches exist at many layers: the browser, a CDN, your server's memory, a shared cache like Redis, and inside the database.

The closer the cache is to the user, the faster it is, and the harder it is to update when data changes.
bridge: React Query's cache is a layer in your browser. The browser's HTTP cache, Netlify's CDN and a Redis cache on the server are the same idea at other layers.

walk.title: Following one product page request through the layers
steps: Browser cache: the user visited 30 seconds ago, and the HTML may be reused or revalidated with a quick 304.
CDN: another user in the same city loaded it recently, so the edge serves it in 10ms.
App memory: the server recently computed the “related products” list and kept it for 60 seconds.
Redis: product details are cached for all server instances to share.
Database: only if every layer above missed does the query actually run.

terms: Found in the cache / had to fetch from the source.
The share of requests answered from the cache.
How long a cached item stays valid.
A cached copy that no longer matches the source.
insights: Add up the TTLs of every layer: that sum is how long a user can see old data after a change, unless you purge.
Never put private data in a shared cache (CDN, reverse proxy, Redis) under a key that does not include the user.
A cache must be optional. When it is empty or down, the app should be slower, not broken.

prod.summary: In production a single page view can be served by four or five caches: browser, CDN, an in-process LRU, Redis and the database buffer cache. Seniors care less about “do we cache” and more about three questions per layer: what is the cache key, who can see the entry (one user or everyone), and what is the worst-case staleness after a write.
checklist: For every cached response, write down the cache key and check it contains everything that changes the output: user or tenant ID, locale, currency, feature-flag variant, auth state.

Responses that depend on cookies or the Authorization header are marked Cache-Control: private (or no-store), and the CDN is configured to respect it. On Amazon CloudFront, a Minimum TTL above 0 makes the CDN cache even private and no-store responses, so personal paths need Minimum TTL 0 (or no caching at all).

Each layer has a known TTL, and the worst-case delay before a change is visible is written down. Without purges it is roughly the Redis TTL plus the CDN TTL (the browser's max-age is counted from when the CDN fetched the copy, through the Age header).
Hit rate is measured per layer: CDN dashboard hit ratio, Redis keyspace_hits / (keyspace_hits + keyspace_misses), and your own hit/miss counters for in-process caches.
In-process caches have a size limit (max entries or max bytes); an unbounded Map used as a cache is a memory leak.
The app still works, slower, when Redis is down: cache calls have a short timeout, errors are caught and logged, and the code falls through to the database.
The database can survive a cold cache (after a deploy, a Redis flush or a CDN purge). Load-test with an empty cache at least once.
numbers: Amazon CloudFront: if you do not use a cache policy and the origin sends no Cache-Control, the default TTL is 24 hours.
Redis hit rate formula from its docs: keyspace_hits / (keyspace_hits + keyspace_misses) * 100, both counters are in INFO stats.
PostgreSQL default shared_buffers (its own page cache) is 128MB; the OS page cache sits under it as one more layer.
failures: Support ticket: “I logged in and saw another customer's name and orders.”

A CDN or reverse proxy cached an authenticated page under a URL-only key. Mark user-specific responses Cache-Control: private, no-store, check the CDN really respects it (CloudFront Minimum TTL must be 0), never cache responses with Set-Cookie, and purge the CDN immediately.
After every deploy the database CPU jumps to 100% for several minutes and p99 latency spikes.
In-process caches start empty on each new pod, so all pods miss at the same time. Use a shared L2 (Redis) under the L1, roll pods out gradually, or warm the hottest keys at startup.
Node pods are OOM-killed every few days; heap grows steadily.
An in-memory cache with no size limit or TTL (often a plain Map keyed by user or query). Use an LRU with max entries and a ttl.
Users in one region see a price change 10 minutes later than others.
Stacked TTLs: Redis TTL plus CDN TTL (plus a little browser time). Purge the CDN on change, keep browser TTL short for data that changes, and document the total staleness budget.
Redis outage takes the whole API down, not just makes it slower.

Cache calls had no timeout and errors were not caught. node-redis also queues commands while disconnected by default, so every request waited for Redis to come back. Disable the offline queue, wrap cache reads with a short timeout (for example 50–100ms) and fall back to the source.

code.title: Two-level cache: in-process LRU (L1) over Redis (L2), Redis optional
code.note: Three lines make Redis optional instead of a hard dependency: the error listener, disableOfflineQueue, and the 50ms timeout around get. The L1 TTL (5 seconds) is much shorter than the Redis TTL because a DEL in Redis cannot reach the memory of other pods.

qs.s: Your product API runs on 12 pods. Each pod has an in-memory cache with a 10-minute TTL. An admin fixes a wrong price, and your code runs DEL product:42 in Redis. What do users see?
o: Some users still get the old price for up to 10 minutes, depending on which pod serves them
Everyone sees the new price immediately, because Redis is the source of truth for the cache
Everyone sees the old price for exactly 10 minutes, then the new one
The pods crash because their cache no longer matches Redis
qs.e: Deleting a Redis key does not touch per-pod memory. Each pod keeps its own copy until its local TTL ends, so results depend on which pod answers. Fix: a very short L1 TTL, or broadcast invalidations (for example Redis pub/sub) to all pods.

qs.s: A Redis cache shows keyspace_hits: 40,000 and keyspace_misses: 360,000. Each miss costs one extra Redis round trip before the DB query. What is the best reading?
o: The cache works well; 40,000 hits saved 40,000 queries
The TTL is too long and should be shortened
Redis needs more memory, more memory always raises hit rate
Hit rate is 10%, so 90% of requests pay an extra round trip for nothing; check the key design and TTL before keeping this cache
qs.e: 40,000 / 400,000 = 10%. A low hit rate means the cache mostly adds latency and staleness. Common causes: keys that include a timestamp or random value, TTL too short for the access pattern, or data that is rarely read twice. More memory only helps when evicted_keys is high.

qs.s: A news site adds Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=300 to its article API. The response includes a “saved by you” flag for the logged-in user. What goes wrong?
o: Nothing; s-maxage only applies to the browser
The browser ignores the header because the user is logged in
The CDN caches the first user's flags and serves them to everyone for 5 minutes
The CDN refuses to cache because the response is JSON
qs.e: s-maxage is for shared caches like CDNs. Any user-specific field makes the response unsafe to share. Split it: a public cached article response plus a small private request for the user's flags.

qs.s: A logged-in user reports seeing someone else's profile. You run this against production. What explains the HIT?

code.title: curl output
code.src:
$ curl -sI https://app.example.com/api/me -H 'Cookie: session=abc...'
HTTP/2 200
content-type: application/json
cache-control: private, no-store
x-cache: Hit from cloudfront
age: 41

o: The browser cached it; x-cache is a browser header
CloudFront always ignores no-store, so this is expected behaviour
The CloudFront cache behavior has a Minimum TTL above 0, which makes it cache even private, no-store responses; set Minimum TTL to 0 for this path and purge
age: 41 means the origin generated a stale response 41 seconds ago
qs.e: CloudFront's docs say that with Minimum TTL > 0 it caches the object for that minimum even when the origin sends no-cache, no-store or private. With Minimum TTL 0 it respects those headers, so “always ignores” is wrong. x-cache and age come from the CDN, not the browser.

qs.s: This report cache runs on each API pod. Users pick any date range. What happens over a week of traffic?

code.title: reports.ts

o: Memory grows with every new user and date range and is never freed, until the pod is OOM-killed; reports also never refresh. Use an LRU with max and ttl
The garbage collector removes entries that have not been read for a while
A Map behaves like an LRU: when it gets large, V8 drops the oldest entries
Nothing bad: the load balancer spreads users across pods, so each Map stays small
qs.e: A Map holds a strong reference to every value, so the garbage collector can never free them. There is no eviction and no TTL, so it is both a memory leak and a staleness bug. Spreading users over pods only slows the growth; every pod still grows without limit.

qs.s: Product data is cached in Redis (TTL 600s, no delete on write). The API response has Cache-Control: max-age=60, s-maxage=300, and the CDN sends a correct Age header. Nobody purges anything. What is the worst-case time before every user sees a price change?
o: 60 seconds, because the browser TTL is the shortest
About 15 minutes (600 + 300 seconds); the browser's 60 seconds is counted from when the CDN fetched the copy, so it does not add more
10 minutes, because Redis is the source the CDN reads from
qs.e: Worst case: Redis was refilled just before the change, so the old value lives 600s. At second 599 the CDN fetches it and keeps it 300s more. Browsers compute freshness as max-age minus Age, so a browser copy never outlives the CDN copy it came from. Adding all three TTLs ignores the Age header.

qs.s: Every API request reads a feature-flag config (2KB). Each pod handles 5,000 req/s. Flags change a few times a day, and 30 seconds of delay after a change is fine. Where should the config be cached?
o: Only in Redis, so all pods always agree
In the CDN, with s-maxage=30
Nowhere: read it from Postgres by primary key on every request
In process memory with a 30-second TTL (or refresh it every 30 seconds in the background)
qs.e: Hot, small, rarely changing data that tolerates 30s of staleness is the ideal in-process case: zero network cost per read. Redis-only would add 5,000 network round trips per second per pod for one tiny value. The CDN does not sit between your server code and its own config, and a DB read per request wastes connections.

interview.q: Walk me through every cache a request can hit in a typical web app. How do you decide which layer a piece of data belongs in?
answer: Layers from the user inward: browser HTTP cache (and service worker), CDN edge, reverse proxy, in-process memory, shared cache like Redis, and the database's own buffer cache plus the OS page cache.
Decide by scope and visibility first: per-user data only in the browser or keyed by user ID on the server; public data can go to the CDN.
Then by read rate vs change rate and staleness budget: static hashed assets in the CDN forever, prices in Redis with short TTL plus delete-on-write, tiny hot config in process memory.
Consider who can invalidate it: you can purge a CDN and delete Redis keys, but you cannot reach browser caches or other pods' memory, so those get short TTLs.
Every layer needs a known key, TTL and owner; measure hit rate per layer and remove caches that do not pay for themselves.

interview.q: We added Redis caching and latency improved, but now Redis failovers and deploys cause outages. How do you make caching safe?
answer: Treat the cache as optional: short command timeouts, no offline queueing, catch errors and fall back to the database.
Protect the database from a cold cache: load-test with an empty cache, roll pods out gradually, warm the hottest keys, and use single-flight so one miss means one query.
Jitter TTLs so keys written together do not expire together.
Use a circuit breaker or rate limit on the fallback path, so a cache outage does not become a database outage.
Alert on hit rate drops, Redis latency and evicted_keys, not only on Redis being down.
followups: What happens to your connection pool when every request falls back to Postgres at once?
Would you use read replicas for the fallback?

interview.q: How do you decide whether a cache is worth keeping?
answer: Measure hit rate per layer. A 10% hit rate means 90% of requests pay an extra round trip for nothing.
Compare the cost of a miss (DB time, external API cost) with the cost of the cache: memory, an extra network hop, invalidation code and staleness risk.
Check the key design: keys with timestamps, random values or very fine-grained parameters never repeat.
Check whether the slow thing can be fixed directly (an index, removing N+1) so no cache is needed.
Look at business impact of staleness: wrong prices or permissions can cost more than the latency saved.
followups: How would you instrument hit rate for an in-process cache?
When is a low hit rate still acceptable?

one: Headers that tell browsers and CDNs whether and how long they may reuse a response.
an: A "best before" date on food, plus a way to ask the shop "is this still the latest batch?" without buying it again.
how: Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable: keep for a year, never re-check (for hashed static files). no-cache: may store, but must revalidate every time. no-store: never store (sensitive data). private vs public: browsers only vs shared caches too. s-maxage: lifetime for shared caches only.
Revalidation: the server sends an ETag (content fingerprint). Next time the browser sends If-None-Match; if unchanged the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body.
stale-while-revalidate=60: serve the stale copy instantly while fetching a fresh one in the background.
why: Correct headers make repeat visits near-instant and cut server load. Wrong ones serve broken old JS after deploys.
trade: A long max-age makes repeat visits instant, but a response already stored in a browser cannot be recalled. Revalidation (no-cache + ETag) keeps content fresh but costs one round trip per use. Hashed file names remove this trade-off for static assets; for HTML and API responses you must choose per route.

myth.r: It forces revalidation. no-store is the one that forbids storing.

q.s: Best headers for index.html in a SPA whose JS files have content hashes?
o: max-age=31536000, immutable
no-cache (or a short max-age) with an ETag, so new deploys are picked up
no-store on everything
No headers
q.e: HTML is the entry point that names the hashed files. It must revalidate; the hashed assets can be cached forever.

Implement ETag on a JSON endpoint and confirm 304s with curl -H 'If-None-Match: ...'.

plain:
HTTP caching headers tell the browser and CDNs whether they may keep a copy of a response, and for how long.

For files whose names change when their content changes (like app.4f3a1c.js), you can say “keep it for a year”. For the HTML page, you say “check with me before using your copy”, which is cheap: if nothing changed, the server answers 304 with no body.
bridge: When you see “(disk cache)” or a 304 status in the DevTools Network tab, these headers are at work. The usual Vite/Next build output already relies on them.

walk.title: A deploy that users see immediately
steps: Your build outputs index.html and assets/app.4f3a1c.js.
Headers: JS gets Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. HTML gets Cache-Control: no-cache plus an ETag.
A user visits: the browser saves both.
You deploy. The new HTML references app.9b21e0.js. On the next visit, the browser revalidates HTML, gets the new version, sees a new JS filename, and downloads it.
If the HTML had been cached for a day, users would keep loading the old app until it expired.

terms: Seconds the response can be reused without asking.
May store, but must check with the server before each use.
Never store at all (for sensitive data).
A content fingerprint; 304 means “your copy is still good”.
insights: Content-hashed file names plus a one-year max-age is the single most effective frontend caching rule.
s-maxage applies only to shared caches such as CDNs. max-age=0, s-maxage=300 lets the CDN keep a page for 5 minutes while browsers revalidate every time.
stale-while-revalidate gives instant responses while refreshing in the background; it trades a little freshness for speed.

prod.summary: In production, HTTP caching is mostly about two rules: content-hashed static assets get max-age=31536000, immutable, and HTML or API responses get either revalidation (no-cache + ETag) or a short, deliberate shared-cache TTL. Seniors read response headers with curl -I before every launch, because a wrong header on index.html can pin users to an old build for days.
checklist: Run curl -sI on the HTML, one JS chunk, one image and one API route in production and read Cache-Control, ETag, Age and the CDN cache-status header.
Only files with a content hash in the name get immutable and a one-year max-age. Files like /logo.png or /sw.js must not.
index.html (and any SPA fallback route) is no-cache or a very short TTL, so a deploy is visible on the next load.
Authenticated or personal responses use private or no-store; never public.
Vary lists only what really changes the body (usually Accept-Encoding). Vary: User-Agent or Vary: Cookie on a CDN destroys the hit rate.
Old hashed chunks stay on the server for some time after a deploy, so users with an open tab can still lazy-load them instead of getting 404 “ChunkLoadError”.
Error responses (500, 502) do not carry long cache headers, or the CDN keeps serving the error after the origin recovers.
numbers: max-age=31536000 is 365 days in seconds, the conventional “forever” value for hashed assets.
Amazon CloudFront honours stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error, but only up to the distribution's maximum TTL.

RFC 9111 allows heuristic caching when no freshness header is sent; it suggests 10% of the time since Last-Modified as a typical value, so a file last changed 10 days ago may be reused for about 1 day without any header.
A 304 Not Modified response has no body, so revalidating a 2MB file costs only headers and one round trip.
failures: After a deploy some users see a white screen; console shows ChunkLoadError: Loading chunk 312 failed or a 404 on /assets/app.4f3a1c.js.
Cached old index.html points at chunk files the new deploy deleted. Serve HTML with no-cache, keep previous build assets for a few days, and reload the page once on chunk-load failure.
Users keep the old logo for weeks after a rebrand.
/logo.png (no hash in the name) was served with max-age=31536000, immutable. Only hashed files may be immutable. Rename the file or add a hash; you cannot recall headers already stored in browsers.
CDN hit ratio is under 5% on static assets.

Cache key includes something that varies per request: a Vary: Cookie header, random query strings like ?t=1716, or a Set-Cookie on asset responses. Remove them and check the CDN's cache-status header goes from MISS to HIT.
A 502 error page stays on the site for an hour after the backend is fixed.
The CDN cached the error response because default or explicit TTLs applied to 5xx. Set short or zero TTL for errors and use stale-if-error to serve the last good copy instead.

code.title: Cache headers for a Vite or Next.js static build
code.note: nginx checks regex locations after finding the longest prefix, and a matching regex wins. ^~ on /assets/ stops that, so hashed SVGs keep immutable. always adds the header to error responses too; without it nginx skips add_header on 4xx/5xx.

qs.s: A response has Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=600. The CDN fetched it 4 minutes ago and sends Age: 240. A browser that has never seen it requests it now. What happens?
o: The CDN goes to the origin, because its copy is older than max-age=60
The CDN serves its copy (fresh for 600s as a shared cache); the browser stores it, but because Age already exceeds 60, the browser must revalidate before reusing it
The CDN serves its copy and the browser reuses it for the next 60 seconds
The browser refuses to store it because s-maxage is present
qs.e: Shared caches use s-maxage (600s), so the CDN copy is still fresh. Browsers use max-age and subtract the Age header: 60 − 240 is below zero, so the stored copy is already stale. The tempting “60 more seconds” answer forgets that Age counts.

qs.s: You read this in production: curl -sI https://shop.example/api/cart returns Cache-Control: public, max-age=300 and x-cache: HIT. What is the risk?
o: A cart is per-user data cached publicly; one user may get another user's cart from the CDN
None; HIT means the CDN is working as intended
Only that the cart may be 5 minutes stale for the same user
The browser will ignore it because carts use POST
qs.e: This is a data leak, not only staleness. A public cache keyed on URL can return one user's cart to another. It should be private, no-store, and the CDN entry must be purged.

qs.s: Your SPA's index.html is served with max-age=86400. You ship a critical bug fix at 10:00. Which statement is true?
o: Users get the fix at once, because the JS file names changed
Users who loaded the page in the last 24 hours may keep running the old build until their cached HTML expires, and a CDN purge does not clear browser caches
A CDN purge fixes it for everyone immediately
Pressing F5 never helps, because the HTML is cached
qs.e: The cached HTML still references the old hashed JS. Purging the CDN only fixes shared caches; browsers keep their copy until max-age ends (a reload revalidates the page, which is one escape). That is why HTML should be no-cache.

qs.s: After this config went live, curl -sI /assets/icons.3f9a2c.svg shows Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600, not the one-year header. Why?

code.title: site.conf

o: In nginx a matching regex location wins over a plain prefix location; use location ^~ /assets/ so the regex is skipped
nginx uses the last add_header in the file, so the order of blocks must be swapped
immutable is not valid for SVG, so nginx falls back to the other header
The CDN rewrote the header; nginx config cannot cause this
qs.e: nginx first finds the longest matching prefix, then checks regex locations in order, and the first matching regex is used. ^~ on the prefix tells nginx not to check regexes. Block order only matters between regex locations, not between a prefix and a regex.

qs.s: Your site runs on two web servers behind a load balancer. Repeat visits never get 304. You capture this traffic. What is wrong?

code.title: request log
code.src:
GET /app/config.json   If-None-Match: "6650a1f2-1c4b"
-> 200 OK   ETag: "6650a1f9-1c4b"   (web-2)

GET /app/config.json   If-None-Match: "6650a1f9-1c4b"
-> 200 OK   ETag: "6650a1f2-1c4b"   (web-1)

o: The browser does not send If-None-Match, so the server cannot answer 304
ETags must be weak (W/) for 304 to work

Each server builds the ETag from the file's modification time and size; the deploy wrote the files a few seconds apart, so the same file has two ETags. Make file times identical across servers or use content-hash ETags
A 304 is not allowed when the response is compressed
qs.e: nginx's ETag is hex(modification time)-hex(length). Same length (1c4b), different time: the file is identical but was copied at different moments. Every request that lands on the other server misses. The log clearly shows If-None-Match is sent, and strong ETags work fine with 304.

qs.s: A price API sends Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=600 through a CDN. Traffic is low: about one request every 5 minutes. The price changed at 10:00. The CDN last fetched at 09:59:30. A user requests at 10:04. What do they get?
o: The new price, because the 60-second freshness has passed
The old price immediately, while the CDN fetches a fresh copy in the background; the next user gets the new price
A 504, because the copy is stale and the CDN must wait for the origin
The new price, after the CDN waits for the origin, marked as stale
qs.e: The copy is 4.5 minutes old: past max-age but inside the 600-second stale window, so the CDN serves it at once and refreshes in the background. On low-traffic URLs this means real staleness can reach max-age + time until the next request. Do not use long SWR windows for data where staleness is costly.

qs.s: An authenticated JSON endpoint returns a large per-user settings object that changes rarely. You want to save bandwidth on repeat loads but never let a shared cache store it. Which header set fits?
o: Cache-Control: public, max-age=60
Cache-Control: no-store plus an ETag, so the browser revalidates
Cache-Control: private, s-maxage=60
Cache-Control: private, no-cache plus an ETag: only the browser stores it, it revalidates every time, and an unchanged object costs a 304 with no body
qs.e: private keeps CDNs out; no-cache allows storing but forces a check, and the ETag turns that check into a cheap 304. With no-store the browser keeps no copy, so there is nothing to revalidate and the ETag is useless. s-maxage is for shared caches, which private excludes.

interview.q: How would you set caching headers for a single-page app deployed behind a CDN? Go file type by file type.
answer: Hashed JS/CSS/fonts/images from the bundler: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. The name changes when content changes, so this is safe.
index.html and SPA fallback routes: no-cache with an ETag (or a very short CDN TTL plus purge on deploy), so a deploy is seen on the next load.
Unhashed public files (/favicon.ico, /robots.txt, /sw.js): short max-age; never immutable. Browsers also check sw.js for updates on their own schedule.
API: public data can use s-maxage plus stale-while-revalidate; personal data private, no-cache or no-store.
Keep old hashed assets for some days after deploy so open tabs can still lazy-load chunks; verify everything with curl -I in production.
followups: How do you handle a ChunkLoadError for users who had the old version open?
What would you do differently for a Next.js app with server rendering?

answer: no-store: no cache may keep a copy at all. Use for sensitive data.
no-cache: a cache may store it but must revalidate with the origin before every use; with an ETag that is a cheap 304.
max-age=0: the copy is stale at once; caches normally revalidate, but without must-revalidate they may serve stale copies in some cases, for example when the origin is unreachable.
must-revalidate: once stale, the copy must not be used without a successful revalidation; if the origin is down, the cache returns an error instead of stale data.
Common mistake: using no-cache when you mean “never store”.

Which one would you use for a bank statement page?

interview.q: After a deploy, some users get a white screen with “ChunkLoadError”. What happened and how do you prevent it?
answer: The user's tab (or a cached index.html) still runs the old build, which tries to lazy-load a chunk the new deploy removed: 404.
Serve HTML with no-cache so new visits get the new build immediately.

one: An in-memory data store used as a cache, session store, rate-limit counter, job queue backend and pub/sub bus.
an: A whiteboard next to your desk: instant to read and write, but not where you keep the company's legal records.
how: Keys map to data structures: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets (leaderboards), streams. Operations like INCR are atomic, which makes counters and rate limits easy.
Every key can have a TTL. When memory fills, an eviction policy (e.g. LRU) removes keys.
Single-threaded command execution, so each command is atomic; Lua scripts or MULTI group several.
why: Sub-millisecond reads for hot data, plus shared state that all your stateless app servers can see.
trade: Memory is expensive, and data can be lost on restart depending on persistence settings (RDB snapshots, AOF). Treat it as a cache or ephemeral state unless you configured it as more. Licensing: in March 2024 Redis moved from BSD to RSALv2/SSPLv1, and the Linux Foundation fork Valkey kept the BSD licence. In May 2025 Redis 8 added AGPLv3, an OSI open-source licence, as an option. Managed services (AWS ElastiCache, Google Memorystore) now offer Valkey too.

myth.m: Redis is my database now, it is faster.
myth.r: Unless you planned for persistence, replication and memory limits, an eviction or restart can silently delete data.

o: The only copy of customer invoices
Per-user rate-limit counters with a 60s TTL
Ten years of analytics events
Full-text search over PDFs
q.e: Short-lived, hot, atomic counters are exactly what it is built for.

lab: Run Redis in Docker and use redis-cli: SET with EX, INCR, a hash, a sorted-set leaderboard (ZADD/ZREVRANGE).
Build cache-aside around a slow function in Node with ioredis or node-redis.
Set maxmemory to 5MB with allkeys-lru, flood keys, and watch evictions in INFO stats.

plain:
Redis is a very fast store that keeps data in memory. You save and read values by key in well under a millisecond.

It is used for caches, sessions, rate-limit counters, job queues, leaderboards and real-time messaging between servers. Because data lives in memory, it is usually treated as temporary, not as the main database.
bridge: Think of it as a giant Map shared by all your servers, with optional expiry on each key, plus extra data types like lists and sorted sets.

walk.title: Caching an expensive query with Redis
steps: Request for the homepage “top products”. Code checks GET top-products in Redis.
Miss: run the 300ms database query, then SET top-products <json> EX 60 (expires in 60 seconds).
The next 1,000 requests in that minute get it from Redis in about 1ms.
After 60 seconds, the key expires automatically. The next request rebuilds it.
When an admin changes a product, the code runs DEL top-products so the change shows up immediately.

terms: Data kept in RAM: very fast, limited in size.
Atomically add 1 to a counter; perfect for rate limits.
Redis deleting keys when memory is full.
insights: Assume any Redis key can disappear (restart, eviction). Your app must work, slower, without it.
Redis runs commands one at a time, so single commands like INCR are safe under concurrency. Two separate commands (GET then SET) are not; use MULTI, a Lua script, or an atomic command.

prod.summary: In production Redis is a shared, single-threaded, in-memory service that every pod depends on. The common outages are not data loss but memory full, one slow command blocking everything (KEYS *, a huge DEL), and connection storms. Seniors set a memory limit and eviction policy, watch latency and evictions, and make the app degrade gracefully when Redis is unreachable.
checklist: maxmemory is set below the container or instance memory (leave room for replication and fork buffers), and maxmemory-policy matches the use: allkeys-lru for a pure cache, noeviction for queues or locks that must not vanish.
Cache data and must-keep data (job queues, sessions) are not in the same instance, or the eviction policy is volatile-* and only cache keys have TTLs.
No KEYS in application code; use SCAN with a COUNT. Large deletes use UNLINK (non-blocking) instead of DEL.
Every cache key has a TTL, and keys are namespaced (app:v2:product:42) so a whole version can be abandoned on a schema change.
Client has connect and command timeouts and a single shared connection (or small pool) per process, not a new connection per request.
Dashboards show used_memory vs maxmemory, evicted_keys, connected_clients, hit rate, and SLOWLOG entries.
Redis is not exposed to the internet, has requirepass or ACL users, and uses TLS on managed services.
numbers: maxmemory default is 0 (no limit) on 64-bit systems; default maxmemory-policy is noeviction.
Default maxclients is 10,000 connections.
SLOWLOG records commands slower than slowlog-log-slower-than = 10,000 microseconds (10ms) by default, keeping the last 128 (slowlog-max-len).
Redis Cluster splits keys into 16,384 hash slots; a multi-key command only works when all keys are in the same slot (use hash tags like {user:42}).
A single string value can be at most 512MB, but values above a few hundred KB already hurt latency for every other client.
failures: Writes fail with OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.
Memory is full and the policy is noeviction (the default). For a cache, switch to allkeys-lru; otherwise find the big keys with redis-cli --bigkeys or MEMORY USAGE and add TTLs.
Every request across all services gets slow for 2–3 seconds, several times a day.
A blocking command on a large dataset: KEYS *, SMEMBERS on a huge set, or DEL of a big key. Check SLOWLOG GET 20, replace with SCAN and UNLINK.
ERR max number of clients reached during a traffic spike.
Code opens a new Redis connection per request, or autoscaling multiplied pods × pool size past 10,000. Reuse one client per process and cap pool size.
Users are logged out after a Redis restart or failover.
Sessions lived in a cache instance with no persistence, or were evicted by allkeys-lru. Put sessions in an instance with AOF and noeviction, or accept re-login as designed.
Rate limiter lets 2× the limit through during bursts.
Code did GET, compared in the app, then SET: two commands, so concurrent requests race. Use INCR (atomic) and read its return value.

code.title: Fixed-window rate limit with atomic INCR (node-redis)
code.note: The decision uses the value returned by INCR, not a separate GET. That single atomic command is what makes it correct when 50 requests from the same user arrive at once.

qs.s: A Redis instance holds both a page cache and the Bull/BullMQ job queues. Memory reaches maxmemory with policy allkeys-lru. What is the real danger?
o: Redis will reject new cache writes with an OOM error
Redis will slow down but nothing is lost
Redis may evict job queue keys, so queued jobs silently disappear
Redis will move old keys to disk automatically
qs.e: allkeys-lru can evict any key, including queue data that was never meant to be temporary. BullMQ's docs ask for noeviction. Put queues and cache in separate instances, each with the right policy. OOM errors would happen with noeviction, not here.

qs.s: You see this in SLOWLOG GET: KEYS session:*, duration 1,800,000 microseconds, every 5 minutes. What is the effect and the fix?
o: Only the cron job that runs it is slow; move it to a replica
Every client is blocked for about 1.8 seconds each time, because Redis runs one command at a time; replace it with SCAN in batches
Redis runs KEYS in a background thread, so it is harmless
It means the session keys have no TTL; add one
qs.e: 1,800,000 microseconds is 1.8 seconds. Command execution is single-threaded, so nothing else runs while KEYS walks the whole keyspace. SCAN returns small pages and lets other commands run between them.

qs.s: Code for a login lockout: const n = Number(await redis.get(k) ?? 0); if (n >= 5) block(); await redis.set(k, n + 1, { EX: 900 });. An attacker sends 50 requests in parallel. What happens?
o: Exactly 5 attempts get through; Redis is single-threaded
No attempts get through because the key is locked during GET
Redis returns an error because SET with EX cannot overwrite a key
Many more than 5 attempts may get through, because many requests read the same old count before any of them writes
qs.e: Each command is atomic, but GET and SET are two commands with app code between them. Parallel requests all read, say, 2, and all pass. Use INCR and check its return value (plus EXPIRE).

qs.s: Since yesterday's release, cache hit rate dropped from 92% to about 61% and DB load went up. You run INFO. What is the best reading?

code.title: redis-cli INFO (excerpt)
code.src:
# Memory
used_memory_human:3.97G
maxmemory_human:4.00G
maxmemory_policy:allkeys-lru
# Stats
evicted_keys:1843220        # yesterday at this time: 1204
keyspace_hits:51200311
keyspace_misses:32733840

o: Redis is unhealthy; restart it to clear memory
Switch to noeviction so Redis stops deleting keys
Lower every TTL to 10 seconds so memory frees faster
The data set no longer fits, so hot keys are evicted before they are read again. Find what grew since the release (redis-cli --bigkeys, MEMORY USAGE on new key patterns) and fix it, or add memory
qs.e: Memory is at the limit and evictions jumped 1,500×: the release added data (new keys without TTL, or bigger values) that pushes useful keys out. noeviction would turn evictions into OOM errors on writes. A restart empties the cache and makes the DB load worse.

qs.s: You moved to Redis Cluster. This code now fails. What is the right fix?

code.title: profile.ts

o: Increase the number of hash slots so both keys fit in one
Use a hash tag so both keys hash on the same part: user:{42}:profile and user:{42}:prefs
Wrap the call in MULTI/EXEC; transactions can span slots
Send the command to the master node instead of a replica
qs.e: Cluster hashes each key to one of 16,384 slots (a fixed number). A multi-key command needs all keys in one slot. With a hash tag, only the text inside {} is hashed, so related keys land together. MULTI has the same same-slot rule, so it fails too.

qs.s: A handler reads 200 small keys one by one with await redis.get(k) in a loop. The network round trip to Redis is 0.5ms and Redis spends about 2µs per GET. Roughly how long does the loop take, and what fixes it?
o: About 0.4ms; Redis is fast, so the loop is fine
About 1 second; Redis is overloaded
About 100ms, almost all network waiting; use one MGET or a pipeline to pay one round trip instead of 200
About 100ms; move the keys to a Lua script so Redis runs them in parallel
qs.e: 200 × 0.5ms = 100ms of round trips; Redis CPU time is only about 0.4ms. Batching (one MGET or pipelining) brings it close to one round trip. Lua would also save round trips, but Redis does not run anything in parallel; it executes one command or script at a time.

qs.s: Sessions live in Redis with appendonly yes and appendfsync everysec. The machine loses power. How much session data can be lost, at most?
o: About the last second of writes
Nothing; AOF writes every command to disk before replying
Everything since the last RDB snapshot, possibly several minutes
All data, because Redis is in-memory only
qs.e: With everysec, Redis calls fsync about once per second, so the Redis docs say you can lose about 1 second of data. Only appendfsync always syncs on every write, and it is much slower. The RDB-only answer would be right without AOF.

interview.q: One Redis instance is used for caching, user sessions and job queues. What problems do you see, and what would you change?
answer: They need different eviction policies: a cache wants allkeys-lru, while sessions and queues must not be evicted (BullMQ requires noeviction).
They need different durability: cache can be lost; sessions and queues need AOF and replication.
Noisy neighbour: one slow command or a memory spike from the cache affects login and jobs.
Split into separate instances (or at least separate databases on managed services with their own limits), each with its own maxmemory and policy.
If you cannot split: volatile-lru with TTLs only on cache keys, plus alerts on memory and evicted_keys.
followups: How would you migrate sessions to a new instance without logging everyone out?
Would you use Redis Cluster here?

interview.q: Design a rate limiter on Redis for 100 requests per minute per user. What are the trade-offs?
answer: Fixed window: INCR on rl:user:minute plus EXPIRE. One round trip, tiny memory, but allows up to 2× the limit around a window boundary.
Sliding window log: a sorted set of timestamps; precise but stores every request (memory grows with the limit).
Sliding window counter or token bucket in a Lua script: smooth and atomic, small memory.
Atomicity is the key point: decide on the value returned by the atomic command, never GET-then-SET in app code.
Decide what happens when Redis is down: fail open (allow) for normal APIs, fail closed for login or payment endpoints.
followups: How do you rate-limit globally across several regions?
Where would you put the limiter: API gateway or app code?

interview.q: Redis latency spikes to hundreds of milliseconds a few times a day. How do you debug it?
answer: Check SLOWLOG GET for slow commands: KEYS, SMEMBERS/HGETALL on huge keys, big DEL.
Use LATENCY DOCTOR / latency monitoring and compare spike times with RDB saves or AOF rewrites: the fork of a large dataset can pause Redis (see latest_fork_usec in INFO).
Check the host: swapping, Transparent Huge Pages (Redis warns about it at startup), noisy neighbours, CPU steal on VMs.
Check the client side: connection storms after deploys, pool exhaustion, large values that take long to transfer.
Find big keys with redis-cli --bigkeys and split them; replace blocking commands with SCAN and UNLINK.
followups: How would you tell server-side latency from network latency?
What would you alert on?

one: Rules for when data enters the cache, when it leaves, and how to avoid serving stale or stampeding.
an: A shop deciding when to restock shelves from the warehouse and when to throw out yesterday's bread.
how: Cache-aside (most common): read cache → on miss read DB → write to cache with a TTL. On update, write DB then delete the cache key.
Write-through: writes go to cache and DB together. Write-behind: write to cache, flush to DB later (fast, risky).
Cache stampede: a hot key expires and 5,000 requests hit the DB at once. Fixes: a lock so only one request recomputes, serving stale while refreshing, or jittered TTLs.
why: Most caching bugs are invalidation bugs: stale prices, users seeing old permissions, outages triggered by one popular key expiring.
trade: TTL-only invalidation is simple and bounded-stale. Event-driven invalidation is fresher but every write path must remember to do it. Pick per data type based on how bad staleness is.

myth.m: Update the cache value on every write instead of deleting it.
myth.r: Two concurrent writers can set the cache in the wrong order and leave stale data forever. Deleting and letting the next read refill is safer.

q.s: The homepage query result is cached with TTL 60s. Every minute, DB CPU spikes to 100% for a few seconds. Cause?
o: Cache stampede when the hot key expires
Replication lag
DNS
q.e: All in-flight requests miss together and recompute. Use a recompute lock or stale-while-revalidate, and jitter TTLs.

more: Cache consistency during DB transactions (invalidate after commit)
lab: Cache a slow query with a 5s TTL. Fire 200 concurrent requests right as it expires and count DB hits.
Add a single-flight lock (Redis SET NX PX) so only one request recomputes; count again.
Add random jitter to TTLs and observe smoother load.
docs: AWS: Database caching strategies using Redis

plain:
Putting data into a cache is easy. Knowing when to throw it away is hard. If you keep it too long, users see old data. If you throw it away too eagerly, the cache does not help.

A special danger: a popular cached item expires, and thousands of requests all try to rebuild it at the same moment, overloading the database (a cache stampede).
bridge: In React Query you call invalidateQueries(['todos']) after a mutation. Server-side caches need the same discipline: every write path must know which cached data it makes stale.

walk.title: Preventing a cache stampede
steps: The homepage data is cached for 60 seconds and requested 2,000 times per second.
At second 60 it expires. In the next 300ms, 600 requests miss and all run the expensive query. The database CPU hits 100%.
Fix 1: a lock. The first request to miss sets a short Redis lock and rebuilds; the others wait briefly or get the old value.
Fix 2: serve the stale value while one background request refreshes it (stale-while-revalidate).
Fix 3: add random jitter to TTLs so many keys do not expire at the same moment.

terms: Removing or updating cached data when the source changes.
App reads cache first; on a miss, reads the DB and fills the cache.
Many requests rebuilding the same expired item at once.
A small random variation added to times to spread them out.
insights: After a write, delete the cache key rather than writing the new value into it. This removes most ordering bugs, but not all: a slow reader can still put an old value back after your delete, so always keep a TTL as a safety net.
Decide per data type how stale is acceptable: prices (seconds), blog posts (minutes), country list (days).
If you cannot explain when a cached item becomes stale, you have a bug waiting to happen.

prod.summary: In production, invalidation is where caching causes incidents: stale prices or permissions, and stampedes that turn one expired key into a database outage. Seniors map every write path to the keys it makes stale, invalidate only after the database transaction commits, keep a TTL on everything as a backstop, and protect hot keys with single-flight recomputation and jittered TTLs.
checklist: Every write path (API, admin panel, background job, migration script) deletes or bumps the version of the cache keys it affects. List them next to the cache key definitions.
Invalidation runs after the DB transaction commits. Deleting inside the transaction lets another request refill the cache with the old row before the commit.
Every key has a TTL even when you invalidate on events, so a missed event heals itself.
Hot keys (requested hundreds of times per second) use a recompute lock or stale-while-revalidate, so one expiry causes one DB query, not hundreds.
TTLs have random jitter (for example ±10%) so keys written together do not expire together.
Authorization data (roles, permissions, feature access) has a very short TTL or is invalidated explicitly; stale permissions are a security bug, not a UX bug.
There is a way to invalidate a whole class of keys at once (a version prefix like v7: or tags) for bad deploys.
numbers: Stampede size is roughly request rate × recompute time: 2,000 req/s × 0.3s query ≈ 600 identical DB queries when one hot key expires without protection.
Redis SET key value NX PX 5000 is one atomic command: it creates a lock only if none exists, with a 5-second expiry so a crashed holder cannot block forever.
With ±10% jitter on a 600-second TTL, expiries spread over a 120-second window instead of one instant.
failures: Admin changes a price; the product page shows the old price for exactly the cache TTL.
The admin panel writes to the DB through a different code path that never deletes the cache key. Centralise writes in one service function that updates the DB and then invalidates.
DB CPU spikes to 100% every N minutes, in step with a cache TTL; p99 latency spikes at the same time.
Cache stampede on a hot key. Add single-flight (a SET NX PX lock or in-process promise sharing), serve stale while one request refreshes, and jitter TTLs.
Rarely, a user keeps seeing old data until the TTL expires, even though invalidation code runs.
Race: request A reads the old row, the writer commits and deletes the key, then A writes the old value into the cache. Invalidate after commit, keep TTLs short for such data, or use versioned keys.
A user removed from a team can still open the team's documents for 15 minutes.
Permissions cached with a 15-minute TTL and no invalidation on membership change. Invalidate the user's permission key on every role change, or do not cache authorization decisions.

code.title: Cache-aside with a safe single-flight lock and jittered TTL
code.note: The lock value is a random token, and the Lua script deletes the lock only if it still holds that token. A plain DEL could remove another caller's lock when load() runs longer than the lock's expiry. Keep the expiry well above the normal load time. db stands for your own data layer.

qs.s: Inside a DB transaction, your code updates a user's email and then deletes user:42 from Redis. The transaction commits 200ms later. Under load, the cache sometimes keeps the old email. Why?
o: Redis DEL is asynchronous and sometimes fails
Between the delete and the commit, another request misses the cache, reads the old (uncommitted change not yet visible) row, and writes it back to the cache
The TTL is too long
Postgres caches the old row in shared_buffers
qs.e: Other transactions cannot see the update until commit, so a reader in that 200ms window refills the cache with the old value. Invalidate after commit (and keep a TTL as a backstop). A long TTL only makes the bug last longer; it is not the cause.

qs.s: A key is read 1,000 times per second. Rebuilding it takes 400ms. It has a fixed 60s TTL and no protection. Roughly how many DB queries run when it expires?
o: About 400
qs.e: Every request that arrives during the 400ms rebuild also misses: 1,000 req/s × 0.4s ≈ 400 identical queries. With a single-flight lock, it would be 1. This is why hot keys need stampede protection.

qs.s: You cache rendered product cards under keys like card:{productId}. A redesign changes the card HTML for all 2 million products. What is the safest way to invalidate?
o: Change the key prefix to card:v2:{productId} and let old keys expire through their TTL
Run KEYS card:* and delete the results
Run FLUSHALL during the deploy
Wait for the TTL; users will get the new design eventually
qs.e: A version prefix invalidates everything at once with no expensive scan; the new code simply never reads old keys. KEYS blocks Redis on a large keyspace, and FLUSHALL also wipes unrelated data and causes a cold-cache stampede.

qs.s: Two admins rename product 7 at almost the same time: A then B in the database. Afterwards the database says “B-name” but the site shows “A-name” for days. Read the code. Why?

code.title: products.ts

o: Redis lost B's write because SET is not atomic

The DB update and the cache update are separate steps, so B's SET reached Redis before A's; A's older value overwrote it. With no TTL it stays wrong until the next rename. Delete the key instead, and always set a TTL
Postgres returned the old row from update
The site reads from a read replica
qs.e: Each admin's DB write and cache write can interleave: A(db), B(db), B(cache), A(cache). The cache ends with the older value, and with no TTL nothing ever repairs it. Deleting on write means the next reader loads the committed row. Each Redis command is atomic; the problem is the ordering of two separate steps.

qs.s: This lock protects a hot key. Rebuilding usually takes 1 second but sometimes 8 seconds. What can go wrong on a slow rebuild?

code.title: rebuild.ts

o: Nothing; NX guarantees only one rebuild ever runs
Redis rejects the DEL because the key already expired
The rebuild is cancelled when the lock expires

After 5s the lock expires, a second caller takes it and starts a rebuild, then the first caller's DEL removes the second caller's lock, so a third can start. Use a unique token, release only if it still matches, and set the expiry above the slow case
qs.e: Lock expiry does not stop the running code; it only lets others in. The plain DEL then deletes a lock the caller no longer owns. Store a random token as the value and release with a compare-and-delete Lua script. DEL of a missing key is not an error; it just returns 0.

qs.s: Logs show thousands of requests per second for /products/<random-id> that do not exist. Your cache-aside code caches only found products. DB CPU is at 90%. What is the most direct fix?
o: Cache “not found” results too, with a short TTL (for example 60s), and reject IDs that are not valid format before any lookup
Increase the TTL of found products
Add more read replicas
Add a single-flight lock on each key
qs.e: Every request uses a different missing ID, so each one misses the cache and hits the database (sometimes called cache penetration). Caching the negative result and validating IDs stops that. Single-flight only merges requests for the same key, so it does not help when every key is different. Longer TTLs only affect keys that exist.

qs.s: Your service commits an order update and then calls redis.del. About once a day Redis is briefly unreachable, the delete fails, and the old value stays until its 1-hour TTL. Staleness of this data matters. Which approach removes this gap?
o: Delete the cache key before the transaction instead of after
Lower the TTL to 1 second

Retry the delete reliably outside the request: write an “invalidate” event in the same DB transaction (outbox), or read the database change log (CDC, for example Debezium on the Postgres WAL) and delete from there
Use FLUSHALL when Redis comes back
qs.e: The invalidation must be as durable as the write. An outbox row is committed with the data and retried until Redis accepts it; CDC gets every committed change from the log. Deleting before the commit opens the race where a reader refills the old value. A 1-second TTL nearly removes caching. FLUSHALL wipes everything and causes a stampede.

interview.q: Design caching for product prices on a shop with 10,000 reads per second and frequent admin edits. How do you keep prices correct?
answer: Cache-aside in Redis keyed by product ID (plus currency/region), with a TTL as a safety net and delete-on-write after commit.
Make invalidation durable: all writes go through one service function, with an outbox or CDC so a failed delete is retried.
Stampede protection on hot products: single-flight lock or stale-while-revalidate, plus jittered TTLs.
Know every layer: in-process caches get seconds of TTL, the CDN gets purged or does not cache prices, browsers revalidate.
At checkout, read the price from the database (source of truth); a cached price is only for display.
followups: What if a flash sale updates 50,000 prices at once?
How do you test that every write path invalidates?

interview.q: What is a cache stampede, and how do you prevent it? Compare the options.
answer: A hot key expires and every concurrent request misses and recomputes it; queries ≈ request rate × rebuild time.
Single-flight lock (SET NX PX with a token): one rebuild, others wait or get stale data; needs careful lock expiry.
Stale-while-revalidate / soft TTL: keep serving the old value while one worker refreshes; best latency, bounded staleness.
Probabilistic early refresh (XFetch): some requests refresh shortly before expiry, so there is never a hard cliff.
Jitter stops many keys expiring together; background refresh fits a small set of known hot keys.
followups: Which one would you pick for a homepage hit 5,000 times per second?
In-process promise sharing vs a Redis lock: when is each enough?

interview.q: Why do teams delete the cache key on write instead of writing the new value? Is delete-on-write fully safe?
answer: Setting the value from two concurrent writers can store the older one last; deleting lets the next reader load the committed row.
Still one race: a reader loads the old row, the writer commits and deletes, then the reader writes the old value back. Rare, but real.
Mitigations: short TTL as a backstop, delayed second delete, versioned values (only write if the version is newer), or leases as described in Facebook's “Scaling Memcache at Facebook” paper.
Invalidate after commit, never inside the transaction.
Pick the strength per data type: permissions and prices need more care than a blog post list.
followups: How would a version number in the cached value help?

diagrams.title: A hot key expires: stampede vs single-flight lock
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Rq as 600 requests
  participant R as Redis
  participant DB as Database
  Note over R: homepage key expires at second 60
  Rq->>R: GET homepage (all miss)
  alt No protection
    Rq->>DB: 600 identical queries
    Note over DB: CPU at 100 percent
  else Single-flight lock
    Rq->>R: SET lock:homepage token NX PX 10000
    R-->>Rq: OK for 1 request, nil for 599
    Rq->>DB: 1 query from the lock holder
    Rq->>R: SET homepage EX 54 to 66s (jitter)
    Rq->>R: 599 others re-check after 100ms
    R-->>Rq: hit
  end
diagrams.caption: What to notice: 2,000 req/s × 0.3s query ≈ 600 misses in the gap. With SET NX, only one request gets the lock and rebuilds; the rest wait briefly and read the fresh value. The ±10% jitter (54–66s for a 60s TTL) stops keys written together from expiring together.

diagrams.title: The race that delete-on-write does not fully fix
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Reader A
  participant C as Redis
  participant DB as Database
  participant W as Writer
  A->>C: GET product:42
  C-->>A: nil (miss)
  A->>DB: SELECT price
  DB-->>A: 10 (old)
  W->>DB: UPDATE price = 12, COMMIT
  W->>C: DEL product:42
  A->>C: SET product:42 price 10
  Note over C: old price stays until the TTL expires
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the writer did everything right (commit, then delete), but a slow reader put the old value back after the delete. This is why every key keeps a TTL as a safety net, even with event-based invalidation.

one: Google's user-centred speed metrics: LCP (loading), INP (responsiveness), CLS (visual stability).
an: Three questions a user feels: did the main thing show up quickly? Did the page react when I tapped? Did stuff jump around while I was reading?
how: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): when the biggest visible image or text block rendered. Good ≤ 2.5s, poor > 4s. Usually the hero image or headline.

INP (Interaction to Next Paint, replaced FID as a Core Web Vital in March 2024): the delay from a click, tap or key press until the next frame is painted. It reports one of the slowest interactions on the page (for pages with many interactions, it ignores one outlier per 50). Good ≤ 200ms, poor > 500ms. Long JavaScript tasks on the main thread are the usual cause.

CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift): how much visible content moves unexpectedly, scored by the largest burst of shifts. Good ≤ 0.1, poor > 0.25. Images without dimensions, late-loading fonts and injected banners cause it.
Google judges each metric at the 75th percentile of real page loads. Measure in the field (real users, CrUX, the web-vitals library), not only in Lighthouse on your fast laptop.
why: They affect search ranking and conversion, and they are the shared language for frontend performance work.
trade: Lab tools (Lighthouse) are reproducible but not reality. Field data (RUM) is reality but noisy and delayed. Use both.

myth.m: A 100 Lighthouse score means the site is fast for users.
myth.r: Lighthouse simulates one device on one network. Your real users on mid-range Android phones on 3G tell the truth.

o: Large images
Long JavaScript tasks on the main thread during interactions (heavy handlers, hydration, re-renders)
DNS TTL
Missing DB index
q.e: INP measures responsiveness. Break up long tasks, reduce re-render work, defer non-critical scripts.

LCP sub-parts: TTFB, resource load delay, load time, render delay

plain:
Core Web Vitals are three numbers Google uses to measure how a page feels to real users.

LCP: how long until the main content appears (good: under 2.5s). INP: how quickly the page responds when you click or type (good: under 200ms). CLS: how much things jump around while loading (good: under 0.1).
bridge: You have seen them in Lighthouse and PageSpeed Insights. The important step up is measuring them from real users' devices, not only your fast laptop.

walk.title: Fixing a product page with poor scores
steps: PageSpeed Insights field data: LCP 4.1s, INP 380ms, CLS 0.25.
LCP: the hero image is discovered late and loads at normal priority. Add fetchpriority="high", preload it, serve a smaller AVIF/WebP version. LCP → 2.2s.
CLS: product images have no width/height, and a cookie banner pushes content down. Add dimensions and reserve banner space. CLS → 0.03.
INP: clicking “Add to cart” re-renders the entire page tree. Memoize the product list, keep the state local to the cart button. INP → 140ms.
Wait 28 days for real-user (CrUX) data to confirm the improvement.

terms: Largest Contentful Paint: when the biggest visible element rendered.
Interaction to Next Paint: delay between a user action and the screen updating.
Cumulative Layout Shift: unexpected movement of content.
Real users' measurements vs a simulated test run.
insights: A normal Lighthouse run loads the page but never clicks, so it cannot measure INP. It reports Total Blocking Time (TBT) as a lab stand-in. A good TBT does not prove a good INP.
INP problems are almost always JavaScript doing too much work on the main thread after an interaction.

prod.summary: In production, Core Web Vitals are a field metric: what matters is the 75th percentile from real users' devices, split by page type and by mobile vs desktop. Seniors send web-vitals data with attribution to their own analytics, so a bad INP points at a specific element and script, and they treat Lighthouse as a quick lab check, not the verdict.
checklist: Real-user monitoring is in place: the web-vitals library (attribution build) sends LCP, INP and CLS with the page template, device type and the element involved.
Dashboards show p75 per page template (home, product, checkout), mobile and desktop separately. One site-wide number hides the bad page.
The LCP element is in the initial HTML, not injected by JavaScript, and has fetchpriority="high"; it is never loading="lazy".
All images, videos, ads and embeds have width and height or a CSS aspect-ratio; banners reserve their space.
Long tasks over 50ms during interactions are found in a DevTools Performance trace; heavy handlers yield to the main thread (scheduler.yield() where supported, or setTimeout).
Third-party scripts (tag managers, chat widgets, A/B testing) are audited for main-thread time; they are often the biggest INP cost.
CI runs Lighthouse with a performance budget to catch regressions before release, but release decisions use field data.
numbers: Thresholds at p75: LCP good ≤ 2.5s (poor > 4s), INP good ≤ 200ms (poor > 500ms), CLS good ≤ 0.1 (poor > 0.25).
CrUX (Chrome UX Report) data in PageSpeed Insights is a rolling 28-day window, so a fix takes up to 4 weeks to show fully.
A “long task” is any main-thread task over 50ms; during it the page cannot respond to input.
INP replaced FID as a Core Web Vital on 12 March 2024.
failures: Search Console: “INP issue: longer than 200ms (mobile)” on product pages, while Lighthouse scores 95.

Lighthouse does not click anything, so it barely measures INP. Use attribution data to find the slow interaction (often “Add to cart” or a filter), then cut the work in the handler, avoid re-rendering the whole tree, and defer analytics calls.
Field LCP is 4.5s on mobile; the LCP element is the hero image.
The image is lazy-loaded, discovered late by JavaScript, or a 2MB JPEG. Put it in the HTML, remove loading="lazy", add fetchpriority="high", serve responsive AVIF/WebP with srcset.
CLS 0.3 only on mobile; users complain they tap the wrong button.
A cookie banner or ad slot is injected above content after load, or web fonts swap with very different metrics. Reserve space with fixed height or aspect-ratio; use size-adjust on fallback fonts.
LCP got worse right after moving the site to client-side rendering.
The LCP element now waits for JS download, parse and a data fetch. Server-render or prerender the above-the-fold content so it is in the first HTML response.

qs.s: Your RUM shows checkout INP p75 = 480ms. The attribution data says: input delay 30ms, processing duration 410ms, presentation delay 40ms, target button#apply-coupon. Where do you look first?
o: The click handler for the coupon button and the re-render it triggers, because almost all the time is spent running event-handler code
Other scripts running before the click, because input delay is the cause
The CSS and layout of the page, because presentation delay is the cause
The network request for the coupon API
qs.e: Processing duration (410ms of 480ms) is the time your event handlers run. Input delay would point at other work blocking the main thread; presentation delay at rendering cost. A network request that is awaited asynchronously does not block the next paint, so it is not counted the same way.

qs.s: You fixed a CLS bug and deployed on 1 May. On 5 May, PageSpeed Insights field data still shows CLS 0.22. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The fix did not work
PageSpeed Insights only measures desktop
CrUX is a rolling 28-day window, so most of the data still comes from before the fix; check your own RUM data for the change
CLS can only be measured in Lighthouse
qs.e: Field data in CrUX aggregates the last 28 days. Four days of good data are mixed with 24 days of old data. Your own web-vitals monitoring shows the change within hours.

qs.s: A product page's LCP element is <img src="hero.avif" loading="lazy"> placed in the initial HTML. Field LCP is 3.8s. What change helps most?
o: Convert the image to PNG for better quality
Remove loading="lazy" and add fetchpriority="high", so the browser starts the download immediately
Add loading="lazy" to all other images too
Move the image into a CSS background so it loads in parallel
qs.e: Lazy-loading the LCP image delays its download until layout confirms it is in the viewport. Removing it and raising priority fixes the delay. A CSS background is discovered even later, so it usually makes LCP worse.

qs.s: Typing in this search box has field INP p75 of 650ms on mobile. products has 20,000 items. Which change fixes INP best?

code.title: ProductSearch.tsx

o: Wrap the filter in useMemo with [products, query] as dependencies
Add loading="lazy" to the images in ProductRow
Let the input update right away and render the list from useDeferredValue(query) in a memoized list component, and virtualize the list so only visible rows are rendered
Preload the JavaScript bundle so the handler is ready sooner
qs.e: Every keystroke re-renders up to 20,000 rows in the same task as the input update, so the next paint waits. useDeferredValue lets React paint the input first and render the list in interruptible background work; virtualization cuts the work itself. useMemo does not help: query changes on every keystroke, so the filter and render run anyway.

qs.s: Field CLS is 0.27 on product pages. Your RUM sends this record. On these pages #product-specs sits directly below the reviews summary, which renders when its own API call returns. What is the right fix?
o: Preload the web fonts
Reserve the space for the reviews summary before its data arrives (fixed min-height or a skeleton of the same size)
Add fetchpriority="high" to the hero image
Lazy-load the reviews widget with an IntersectionObserver
qs.e: largestShiftTarget names the element that moved, not the one that caused the move. The biggest shift (0.24 of 0.27) happens at 3.2s, after the page fully loaded: the specs block was pushed down when the reviews summary above it appeared with no reserved space. Reserving that space removes the shift. Font swaps happen early in the load and shift text. Lazy-loading still inserts the widget without space, so it still shifts.

qs.s: Mobile RUM for a page, 1,000 loads: 70% have LCP ≤ 2.3s, 78% ≤ 2.5s, 85% ≤ 3.0s. Does the page pass the LCP “good” threshold?
o: No: 22% of loads are slower than 2.5s, and Google needs all loads under 2.5s
No: the average must be under 2.5s and slow loads pull it above
It cannot be known without Lighthouse
Yes: the 75th percentile is at or below 2.5s, because 78% of loads are ≤ 2.5s
qs.e: Core Web Vitals are judged at p75. If 78% of loads are ≤ 2.5s, the 75th-percentile value is ≤ 2.5s, so it is “good”. A quarter of users can still have a slow page and the metric passes; that is why teams also watch p90 for their own goals.

qs.s: Your Next.js app uses client-side navigation. A user lands on /, then clicks to /products and /cart without full page loads. How do the standard web-vitals library and CrUX report this visit?
o: As one page load for /: LCP comes from the landing page only, while INP and CLS cover the whole visit, including interactions and shifts on later routes
As three page loads, each with its own LCP, INP and CLS
Only /cart is reported, because the last URL wins
Nothing is reported, because SPAs do not support Web Vitals
qs.e: Soft (client-side) navigations are not new page loads to the browser. LCP stops at the first interaction, but INP and CLS keep collecting until the page is hidden, and everything is reported against the landing URL. So a slow cart button can show up as poor INP on /. Chrome's soft navigation reporting is still experimental.

interview.q: Our INP is poor on mobile. How would you find and fix the cause?
answer: Start from field data with attribution: which page template, which element (interactionTarget), and which phase is large: input delay, processing duration or presentation delay.
Input delay points at other main-thread work at the time of the click (hydration, third-party scripts); processing at the handlers; presentation at rendering and layout cost.
Reproduce in DevTools Performance with CPU throttling (4× or 6×) and look at the long task; Long Animation Frames data shows which script ran.
Fixes: do less in the handler, show feedback first and defer the rest (scheduler.yield(), React transitions), avoid re-rendering large trees, virtualize long lists, audit third-party scripts.
Verify with your own RUM within days; CrUX takes up to 28 days to reflect it.

interview.q: How would you set up performance monitoring for a large site? Lab vs field.
answer: Field (RUM): web-vitals with attribution sent to your analytics, split by template, device class and country, reported at p75.
CrUX / Search Console as the external view Google uses; it lags by up to 28 days and only covers sites with enough Chrome traffic.
Lab: Lighthouse CI or WebPageTest in the pipeline with budgets (bundle size, TBT, LCP on a throttled profile) to catch regressions before release.
Lab is reproducible but not real; field is real but noisy and delayed. Release decisions use field, regression gates use lab.
Alert on p75 changes per template after deploys, and tag RUM data with the release version.

Why might lab and field LCP disagree?

interview.q: How would you improve LCP on an image-heavy product page?
answer: Break LCP into its parts: TTFB, resource load delay, resource load duration and element render delay; fix the biggest part.
TTFB: CDN caching of HTML, faster server rendering, fewer redirects.
Load delay: the LCP image must be in the initial HTML, not lazy, with fetchpriority="high" or a preload; not a CSS background discovered late.
Load duration: responsive srcset, AVIF/WebP, right size for the device, served from a CDN close to the user.
Render delay: render-blocking CSS, fonts, or client-side rendering that waits for JS; server-render the above-the-fold content.

one: Measuring where time actually goes before optimising anything.
an: A doctor runs tests before operating. Guessing which organ hurts gets people killed.
how: Backend: APM traces show time per span (DB, HTTP calls, code). Database: EXPLAIN ANALYZE, slow query logs, pg_stat_statements. CPU: flame graphs show which functions burn time.
Frontend: Chrome DevTools Performance panel (long tasks, layout thrash), React Profiler (wasted renders), Network panel (waterfalls, blocking resources), bundle analyzers.
Look at percentiles. p50 hides the pain; p95 / p99 is what your unluckiest users and your busiest customers feel.
why: Optimisation without measurement wastes days on code that was never the bottleneck. Amdahl's law: speeding up a part that is 5% of the time can gain at most 5%.
trade: Profiling in development misses production data sizes and concurrency. Production profiling needs low-overhead tools (sampling profilers, tracing).

myth.m: The average response time is 120ms, so we are fine.
myth.r: If p99 is 4 seconds, 1 in 100 requests is terrible, and a page making 20 requests hits it often.

q.s: A page makes 30 API calls. Each call's p99 is 1s, while p50 is 80ms. Roughly how often does a page load include at least one slow call?
o: About 1%
Never
Always
q.e: Tail latency compounds with fan-out. This is why seniors watch p99 and reduce call counts.

pg_stat_statements to find the most expensive queries overall
