plain:
Profiling means measuring where time actually goes before you try to make anything faster. Developers are famously bad at guessing the slow part.

Look at percentiles, not averages: p95 is the time that 95% of requests are faster than. The slowest few percent are where users get frustrated.
bridge: The DevTools Performance panel and the React Profiler are profilers. The backend has equivalents: request traces, database query statistics and CPU flame graphs.

walk.title: Finding why checkout is slow
steps: Dashboard: checkout p50 is 400ms, but p95 is 3.2s.
Open a trace of a slow checkout request. It shows the spans: auth 5ms, load cart 20ms, tax API 2.8s, save order 30ms.
The tax API call is the bottleneck, not your code or database.
It runs on every checkout even though tax rates rarely change. Cache rates for 10 minutes and add a 1-second timeout with a fallback.
p95 drops to 450ms. Rewriting your own code, which you first suspected, would have gained almost nothing.

terms: The time that 50% / 95% / 99% of requests are faster than.
A timeline of one request / one timed step inside it.
A chart showing which functions use the most CPU time.
The one slowest part that limits everything.
insights: Open the trace of a slow request (p95 or p99), not a typical one. The average request rarely contains the problem.
Production data sizes and traffic reveal problems that development never shows.

prod.summary: In production, profiling starts from a symptom in metrics (p95 or p99 latency, CPU, a bad Web Vital) and narrows down with the cheapest tool that can answer: a distributed trace to find the slow span, pg_stat_statements for the database, a CPU profile or flame graph for code, a heap snapshot for memory. Seniors insist on numbers before and after every optimisation, measured on production-like data.
checklist: The problem is stated as a number on a percentile: “checkout p95 is 3.2s, target 800ms”, not “checkout is slow”.
A trace of a slow request (not an average one) is opened, and the biggest span is identified before anyone edits code.
pg_stat_statements is enabled, and the top queries by total_exec_time are reviewed; a 5ms query called 2 million times can matter more than one 3s query.
Slow-query logging is on with a sensible threshold (log_min_duration_statement, for example 500ms); it is off by default.
CPU-bound Node services are profiled with --cpu-prof or a sampling profiler under realistic load, and event-loop delay is monitored (perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay).
Memory leaks are checked with two heap snapshots taken minutes apart, comparing which object types grew.
After the fix, the same percentile is measured again under the same load, and the result is recorded in the PR.
numbers: PostgreSQL log_min_duration_statement defaults to -1 (disabled); pg_stat_statements needs shared_preload_libraries and a restart, and tracks up to 5,000 statements by default (pg_stat_statements.max).
Tail fan-out: with 30 parallel calls each having a 1% chance of hitting p99, 1 − 0.99<sup>30</sup> ≈ 26% of page loads include a slow call.
Chrome marks main-thread tasks over 50ms as long tasks (red corner in the Performance panel).
Amdahl's law: if a part is 20% of total time, making it infinitely fast saves at most 20%.
failures: p50 is fine, p99 is 5× higher, and only for some customers.

Large tenants hit code paths with N+1 queries or unindexed filters that small test accounts never exercise. Pull traces for those tenants and run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) with their real parameters.
Node service: latency rises with load while CPU sits at 100% on one core and the DB is idle.
Synchronous work blocks the event loop: JSON.parse of large payloads, sync crypto, regex backtracking. A CPU profile shows the hot function; move it to a worker thread or make it smaller.
Memory grows steadily until the pod is OOM-killed; restarts “fix” it for a day.
A leak: a module-level cache or listener array that is never cleared. Compare two heap snapshots and look at the retainers of the growing objects.
The team spent a week optimising a function; end-to-end latency did not change.
Nobody profiled first; the function was a few percent of request time. Start from a trace of real slow requests and work on the biggest span.

code.title: Find the queries that cost the most in total (PostgreSQL 16/17)
code.src:
-- postgresql.conf: shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'  (then restart)
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;

SELECT
  round(total_exec_time::numeric / 1000, 1)            AS total_sec,
  calls,
  round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2)                    AS mean_ms,
  round((100 * total_exec_time / sum(total_exec_time) OVER ())::numeric, 1) AS pct,
  left(query, 80)                                      AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- After a fix, reset counters and compare the same period:
-- SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset();
code.note: Sort by total_exec_time, not mean_exec_time: the most expensive query overall is often a fast one called millions of times. The pct column tells you the maximum you can gain (Amdahl's law). The ::numeric casts are required: Postgres has no two-argument round() for double precision.

qs.s: pg_stat_statements shows: query A, 1 call/hour, mean 4,000ms; query B, 3,000,000 calls/day, mean 3ms. Which should you optimise first to reduce database load?
o: Query A, because it is over 1,000 times slower
Neither; both are under 5 seconds
Query A, because slow queries cause locks
Query B: it uses about 9,000 seconds of DB time per day versus about 96 seconds for A
qs.e: Total time is what loads the database: 3,000,000 × 3ms = 9,000s per day, versus 24 × 4s = 96s for A. A may still matter for one user's latency, but for load, B is the target.

qs.s: A Node API's p99 grows from 80ms to 2s under load. The database shows low CPU and fast queries. Event-loop delay p99 is 1.5s. What is the most likely cause?
o: Synchronous CPU work in request handlers is blocking the event loop, so every request waits in line
The database connection pool is too small
The network between app and DB is slow
The load balancer is misconfigured
qs.e: Event-loop delay of 1.5s means JavaScript could not run anything else for that long. A pool that is too small shows as waiting for a connection with an idle event loop. Take a CPU profile under load to find the blocking function.

qs.s: Checkout has 5 sequential steps taking 40ms, 60ms, 900ms, 50ms and 30ms. A teammate proposes making the 60ms step 10× faster. What is the maximum end-to-end gain?
o: About 10×, because the step becomes 10× faster
About 50%
54ms, about 5% of the 1,080ms total; the 900ms step is the real bottleneck
None, because sequential steps cannot be optimised
qs.e: 60ms → 6ms saves 54ms out of 1,080ms (5%). Amdahl's law: the gain is limited by that step's share of the total. Profile and attack the 900ms step first.

  Filter: ((customer_id = 4821) AND (status = 'open'::text))
  Rows Removed by Filter: 2399991
  Buffers: shared hit=2210 read=22000
Planning Time: 0.112 ms
Execution Time: 812.502 ms

o: Increase shared_buffers, because most pages were read from disk
Run VACUUM ANALYZE, because the planner's estimate is wrong
Add LIMIT 50 to the query
Add an index on (customer_id, status): Postgres reads 2.4 million rows to return 9
qs.e: “Rows Removed by Filter: 2399991” for 9 results means a full table scan. An index turns it into a few page reads. More cache would make the same useless scan a bit faster. The estimate (12 rows) is close to the real 9, so statistics are fine. LIMIT does not help when only 9 rows match; the scan still reads the whole table.

qs.s: Login p99 is 2s under load. CPU is 100% on one core, the DB is idle. A --cpu-prof profile (bottom-up, self time) shows this; you expand the top row to see its callers. What is the best fix?

code.title: CPU profile, bottom-up (self time)
code.src:
Self time   Function          Source
  58.9%     _encipher         bcryptjs/index.js
   9.2%     JSON.stringify    (native)
   6.0%     (garbage collector)
   2.5%     _key              bcryptjs/index.js
   ...

Callers of _encipher (expanded):
_encipher <- _key <- next <- _crypt <- _hash <- hashSync <- compareSync <- login  src/auth.ts:18

o: Increase the database connection pool size
Stop hashing on the main thread: use the async API of the native bcrypt package (it runs in the libuv thread pool) or a worker thread, and size the pool for login traffic
Lower the bcrypt cost factor to 4 so hashing is fast
Give the pod more memory
qs.e: The self time sits in bcryptjs internals (_encipher); its caller chain shows they all come from compareSync in the login handler. compareSync blocks the event loop for every login, so all other requests wait behind it. Moving it off the main thread lets the process use more cores and keep serving. A cost factor of 4 would make password cracking much easier, a security regression. The DB is idle, so the pool is not the limit. Note the libuv pool has 4 threads by default (UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE).

qs.s: You have 10 API pods. Each reports its own p99 latency. The dashboard shows the average of the ten p99 values: 200ms. What is the fleet-wide p99?
o: 200ms, the average of the p99s
The highest of the ten p99s

It cannot be computed from these numbers; percentiles cannot be averaged. Record latency histograms on each pod, sum the buckets, and compute the percentile from the total (for example histogram_quantile over summed buckets in Prometheus)
The median of the ten p99s
qs.e: A percentile depends on the full distribution. One busy, slow pod with most of the traffic can make the real p99 much higher than the average of p99s, and an idle pod's p99 counts the same in an average. Histograms can be added together; percentiles cannot.

qs.s: Heap grows about 50MB per hour on a Node service and logs show this warning. What is the cause and fix?

code.title: service log + code

o: Each request adds a listener that is never removed, so closed connections stay referenced. Remove it on disconnect: req.on('close', () => prices.off('price', onPrice))
Call prices.setMaxListeners(0) to remove the limit; the warning is a false alarm
Raise --max-old-space-size so the heap has room
Nothing; the garbage collector frees listeners when the response ends
qs.e: The emitter holds a reference to every onPrice, and each closure holds its res, so nothing from closed clients can be collected. The warning is exactly this leak. Removing the limit hides the warning and keeps the leak; a bigger heap only delays the OOM. The GC cannot free objects that are still referenced.

interview.q: An endpoint's p99 doubled after last week's release. Walk me through how you find the cause.
answer: Confirm and scope it: which endpoint, which percentile, since which deploy, all customers or some, all pods or some.
Compare traces of slow requests before and after: which span grew (DB, external call, own code, waiting for a connection).
For DB spans: pg_stat_statements diff for that period, then EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) with the slow customers' real parameters.
For own code: CPU profile under load and event-loop delay; for memory: GC time and heap growth.
Read the release diff with the slow span in mind; fix, then measure the same percentile under the same load and record it.
followups: What if no single span grew, but everything got a little slower?
How do you get traces for p99 requests when you sample 1%?

interview.q: How do you profile a Node.js service in production safely?
answer: Prefer sampling profilers with low overhead: continuous profiling (for example Pyroscope or Datadog) or a short --cpu-prof / inspector session on one pod.
Watch cheap signals all the time: event-loop delay (monitorEventLoopDelay), GC time, heap used, active handles.
Heap snapshots pause the process and need extra memory about the size of the heap; take them on one pod removed from the load balancer.
Reproduce with production-like data and traffic when possible; small test data hides N+1 and scaling problems.
Never profile every pod at once, and make sure profiles do not leak secrets (they can contain strings from memory).
followups: Sampling vs instrumenting profilers: when would you use each?
How do you read a flame graph?

interview.q: Why are averages misleading for latency, and how should latency be measured and aggregated?
answer: Latency is skewed: a few very slow requests are hidden in an average. Use p50 for the typical case and p95/p99 for the tail.
Tail latency grows with fan-out: a page with 30 calls hits some call's p99 on about 26% of loads.
Record histograms, not pre-computed percentiles, so data from many pods and time ranges can be combined correctly.
Load tests must avoid coordinated omission (the test tool waiting for slow responses before sending the next request), or they report a falsely good tail.
Set SLOs on percentiles (“p99 under 500ms for 99.9% of minutes”) and alert on their burn rate.
followups: How would you reduce tail latency in a service that fans out to 20 backends?
